name: Philip Pullman
milestone_by_age_26: Debut novel The Haunted Storm (1972) was joint-winner of the New English Library's Young Writer's Award, published when Pullman was 25.
early_history_summary: Pullman grew up in a peripatetic RAF family, moving between England, Rhodesia, and Australia after his father's death in a plane crash in 1954. He studied English at Exeter College, Oxford, and began teaching at Oxford middle schools at age 25, during which time he wrote and published his first novel.
family_context_summary: Son of an RAF pilot killed in a plane crash in 1954 when Pullman was seven; his grandfather was a Church of England rector who instilled a love of storytelling. His mother remarried another RAF pilot, and the family moved frequently.
parent_family_domain_summary: His grandfather, an Anglican rector, was a master storyteller who significantly influenced Pullman's narrative imagination. No evidence of parental literary profession.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Oxford education, grandfather storyteller, father's death
evidence_summary: Pullman's debut novel won a minor award at age 25, but his major fame came decades later with His Dark Materials (1995-2000). His early advantages were modest: an Oxford English degree and a storytelling-inclined grandfather. His father's death and frequent childhood moves created adversity but also exposure to diverse cultures. No evidence of significant family wealth or literary networks.
starting_point: Born in Norwich in 1946 to an RAF pilot father and a mother who remarried another RAF pilot after his father's death in 1954; family moved between England, Rhodesia, and Australia.
current_position: Sir Philip Pullman is one of Britain's most celebrated living authors; published The Rose Field in October 2025 completing The Book of Dust trilogy; was knighted in 2019; lives in Oxford.

trajectory.event: Debut novel The Haunted Storm published and jointly won the New English Library's Young Writer's Award.
Published first children's book, Count Karlstein.
Published The Ruby in the Smoke, the first Sally Lockhart novel, which led him to stop teaching.
Published Northern Lights (The Golden Compass), first volume of His Dark Materials, winning the Carnegie Medal.
The Amber Spyglass won the Whitbread Book of the Year Award, the first children's book to do so.
Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to literature.
Published The Rose Field, completing The Book of Dust trilogy.

name: Jane Hawking
milestone_by_age_26: No material writing milestone by age 26; Jane Hawking married Stephen Hawking at 21 and was primarily a caregiver and teacher. Her first book was published in 1999 at age 55.
early_history_summary: Jane Wilde studied languages at Westfield College, London, and met Stephen Hawking in 1962. They married in 1965 when she was 21. She spent her twenties and thirties as Stephen's primary caregiver while raising three children, only completing her PhD in medieval Spanish poetry in 1981 at age 37.
family_context_summary: Born to George and Beryl Wilde in St Albans, Hertfordshire. Family background not extensively documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Jane Hawking's public profile derives entirely from her marriage to Stephen Hawking. She had no published writing or independent career milestone by age 26. Her first book, Music to Move the Stars, was published in 1999 when she was 55. Her PhD was completed at age 37. She is ineligible as no material milestone by age 26 is documented.

name: Hana Mandlíková
milestone_by_age_26: Won first Grand Slam singles title at the 1980 Australian Open at age 18, defeating Wendy Turnbull in straight sets; by age 26 she had won four Grand Slam titles and reached world No. 3.
early_history_summary: Mandlíková was born in Prague to Olympic sprinter Vilém Mandlík and came to tennis prominence as a junior, winning the 1977 Orange Bowl at age 15. In 1978, she became the first female world No. 1 junior and won her first WTA titles at age 16. She won her first Grand Slam at the 1980 Australian Open at 18.
family_context_summary: Born in Prague to Vilém Mandlík, a Czechoslovak Olympic 200-metre semi-finalist at the 1956 and 1960 Olympics, providing direct athletic pedigree and exposure to competitive sport from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Olympic father, Czech tennis system, early junior success, club coaches
evidence_summary: Mandlíková's father was an Olympic sprinter, giving her elite athletic genetics and direct exposure to competitive sport. The Czechoslovak sports system provided structured training from a young age, with Hall of Fame club coaches Imre Sarosi and Steffen Hunyadfi. She won the Orange Bowl at 15, became the first world No. 1 junior at 16, and won her first Grand Slam at 18. Her early trajectory was defined by deep athletic inheritance and an intensive junior pipeline.
starting_point: Born in Prague in 1962 to Vilém Mandlík, an Olympic 200-metre sprinter who competed at the 1956 and 1960 Olympics, providing elite athletic pedigree.
current_position: Retired professional tennis player with 4 Grand Slam singles titles; inducted into International Tennis Hall of Fame in 1994; later coached Jana Novotná to the Wimbledon title; became an Australian citizen.

trajectory.event: Won the Orange Bowl junior tournament, establishing herself on the international tennis map.

name: Yoshinori Ohsumi
milestone_by_age_26: No material research milestone by age 26; Ohsumi was a graduate student at the University of Tokyo through his mid-twenties. His Nobel-winning autophagy discoveries came in the 1990s when he was in his late forties.
early_history_summary: Ohsumi grew up in post-WWII Japan, influenced by his father who was an engineering professor at Kyushu University. He entered the University of Tokyo to study chemistry but switched to molecular biology, joining Kazutomo Imahori's lab as a graduate student. He struggled to find a good position in Japan and took a postdoc at Rockefeller University with Gerald Edelman in the mid-1970s.
family_context_summary: Son of a professor of engineering at Kyushu University; grew up familiar with academic life in post-war Japan. His elder brother was also a researcher.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an engineering professor at Kyushu University, providing exposure to academic life and lowering the psychological barrier to a research career.
evidence_summary: Ohsumi had an academic upbringing (father was an engineering professor) and entered the University of Tokyo, but by age 26 he was still a graduate student with no major published breakthrough. His Nobel Prize-winning work on autophagy came decades later, beginning with yeast experiments in the late 1980s and key discoveries in the 1990s. He is ineligible as no material milestone by age 26 is documented.

name: Katalin Szőke
milestone_by_age_26: Won two Olympic gold medals at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics at age 16 (100m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay), both in world record time; also won two European Championship golds in 1954.
early_history_summary: Szőke was born in Budapest to an Olympic water polo champion father and a Hungarian swimming champion mother. She started swimming at six months and competing at age six. By twelve, she was one of Hungary's premier freestyle swimmers. At 16, she won two Olympic gold medals at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics in world record time.
family_context_summary: Born to Márton Homonnai, a two-time Olympic champion in water polo (1932, 1936), and Katalin Szőke, a Hungarian swimming champion. Both parents were elite athletes, providing extraordinary athletic pedigree and early immersion in competitive swimming.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Olympic parents, Hungarian swimming system, early start, Hall of Fame coaches, post-war adversity
evidence_summary: Szőke's both parents were champion athletes — her father a two-time Olympic water polo gold medalist and her mother a national swimming champion. She started swimming at six months and competing at six, coached by Hall of Famers Imre Sarosi and Steffen Hunyadfi within the world-dominant Hungarian women's swimming program of the 1950s. She won Olympic gold at 16, benefiting from an extraordinary combination of genetic endowment, parental domain expertise, and an elite national sports pipeline. Her father's wartime collaboration and flight added family adversity.
starting_point: Born in Budapest in 1935 to Márton Homonnai, a two-time Olympic water polo champion, and Katalin Szőke, a Hungarian swimming champion; started swimming at six months and competing at age six.
current_position: Died on October 27, 2017 at age 82 in Los Angeles, California; final status: two-time Olympic gold medalist (1952), two-time European champion (1954), inducted into International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1985.

trajectory.event: Won two Olympic gold medals at the Helsinki Olympics in the 100m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay, both in world record time.

name: Israel Adesanya
milestone_by_age_26: Won three King in the Ring eight-man kickboxing tournaments in New Zealand (August 2014, April 2015, October 2015) by age 26, amassing a professional kickboxing record of approximately 50-2 and winning the WKBF New Zealand Cruiserweight Championship.
early_history_summary: Born in Lagos, Nigeria to an accountant father and nurse mother, Adesanya moved to New Zealand at age 10. He experienced racist bullying in high school and started training in kickboxing at 18 after watching the film Ong-Bak. He compiled a 32-0 amateur kickboxing record before turning professional in 2010, and moved to Auckland at 21 to train at City Kickboxing under Eugene Bareman.
family_context_summary: Born into a relatively comfortable upper-middle-class Nigerian family in Lagos; father is an accountant, mother is a nurse. Family relocated to New Zealand for better educational opportunities when Adesanya was 10.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bullying catalyst, City Kickboxing gym, Eugene Bareman, late start, natural talent
evidence_summary: Adesanya started kickboxing relatively late at 18, motivated by racist bullying he experienced after moving from Nigeria to New Zealand. He found a high-quality training environment at City Kickboxing in Auckland under coach Eugene Bareman, alongside future UFC fighters Dan Hooker and Kai Kara-France. His family was middle-class (father an accountant, mother a nurse), providing some financial stability. His natural physical talent (6'4", 80-inch reach) and 32-0 amateur record suggest innate ability. His major UFC fame came after age 28, but by 26 he had established himself as a dominant regional kickboxer.
starting_point: Born in Lagos, Nigeria in 1989 to an accountant father and nurse mother in a relatively comfortable upper-middle-class household; family relocated to New Zealand at age 10 for better education.
current_position: Former two-time UFC middleweight champion; still competing in the UFC middleweight division as of 2025; widely regarded as one of the best strikers in MMA history.

Regained the UFC middleweight title by knocking out Alex Pereira at UFC 287.
Continued competing in the UFC middleweight division.

name: Trixi Schuba
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1972 Olympic gold medal in ladies' figure skating at Sapporo at age 21; also won World and European championships in both 1971 and 1972, and was six-time Austrian national champion (1967-1972).
early_history_summary: Schuba started skating at age four after seeing a skating competition on television. She was coached by Helmut Seibt from 1955 to 1962 and then by Leopold Linhart. She became Austrian national champion at 16 in 1967 and steadily improved, winning European and World championships in 1971 and 1972, culminating in Olympic gold at Sapporo in 1972. She was renowned as one of the greatest compulsory figures skaters in history.
family_context_summary: Parents owned a wood business in Vienna. Her father died when she was 11, and she helped her mother with the business while continuing skating training and accounting studies.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Early start at 4, sustained coaching, Vienna Eislaufverein, compulsory figures specialist, father's death
evidence_summary: Schuba started skating at age four and was coached continuously by high-quality coaches (Helmut Seibt, then Leopold Linhart) for over 15 years before her Olympic victory. Her family owned a wood business in Vienna, providing modest financial stability, though her father's death when she was 11 forced her to balance training with helping the family business and accounting studies. She was widely acknowledged as one of the supreme artists of compulsory figure skating, a specialized skill that dominated competition scoring in her era. Her sustained coaching from childhood was a key advantage.
starting_point: Born in Vienna in 1951 to parents who owned a wood business; started skating at age four after seeing a skating competition on the family's new television.
current_position: 1972 Olympic gold medalist; former president of the Austrian Figure Skating Association (2002-2006); vice-president of the Graz Skating Association; worked for Vienna Insurance Group attending to UN diplomats.

trajectory.event: Won her first Austrian national ladies' figure skating championship.

name: Ryszard Szurkowski
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Peace Race (the 'amateur Tour de France') in 1970 at age 24 and again in 1971 at age 25; also won the Polish cyclo-cross championship in 1968 at age 22.
early_history_summary: Born in the small village of Świebodów in post-war Poland, Szurkowski came from a working-class family. He began cycling at 17 in 1963 as an unattached amateur, worked as a postman delivering mail by bicycle, and was largely self-taught. He first gained prominence by winning the Polish cyclo-cross championship in 1968, then won the prestigious Peace Race in 1970 and 1971, establishing himself as the dominant amateur cyclist in Eastern Europe.
family_context_summary: Born in the small village of Świebodów in Lower Silesia to a working-class family; his father was not documented. He worked as a rural postman delivering mail by bicycle as a young man. His grandmother was an early supporter, occasionally giving him money for inner tubes.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Working-class background, self-taught, postman by bicycle, rural Poland, brother's encouragement
evidence_summary: Szurkowski came from a poor, working-class background in rural Poland with no family cycling tradition. He was largely self-taught, starting competitive cycling at 17 and working as a postman delivering mail by bicycle, which provided natural cycling exposure. His older brother Czesław encouraged him to continue after military service. He joined the KS Dolmel Wrocław club, which gave him access to the Polish amateur cycling pipeline. His rise from rural poverty to winning the Peace Race at 24 exemplifies constraint-driven self-creation, with limited inherited advantages.
starting_point: Born in 1946 in the small village of Świebodów, Lower Silesia, Poland, to a working-class family; worked as a rural postman delivering mail by bicycle as a young man.
current_position: Died on February 1, 2021 at age 75 in Radom, Poland; final status: legendary Polish road cyclist, four-time Peace Race winner, World champion (1973), two-time Olympic silver medalist, voted second-greatest Polish athlete of the 20th century.

name: Juan Martín del Potro
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2009 US Open at age 20, defeating Rafael Nadal in the semifinals and five-time defending champion Roger Federer in the final; also won four consecutive ATP titles in 2008 at age 19-20, the first player in ATP history to win his first four titles in as many tournaments.
early_history_summary: Del Potro was born in Tandil, Argentina, a small city that produced an unusual number of professional tennis players. He started playing tennis at age seven under coach Marcelo Gómez, who also coached other Tandil ATP pros. He won the Orange Bowl 14s title at 14, reached No. 3 in the ITF junior rankings, and won his first ATP title at 19. His breakthrough came at the 2009 US Open where he defeated both Nadal and Federer to win his first Grand Slam at age 20.
family_context_summary: Born in Tandil, Argentina to Daniel del Potro, a semi-pro rugby player and veterinarian, and Patricia Lucas, a teacher. Middle-class family; father later misappropriated $30 million of his career earnings. Has a younger sister and a deceased elder sister.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Tandil tennis pipeline, Marcelo Gómez coaching, athletic father, early junior success, physical stature
evidence_summary: Del Potro benefited from Tandil's extraordinary tennis pipeline, where coach Marcelo Gómez trained multiple ATP professionals from a city of 100,000. He started at age seven with Gómez and was coached by him for over a decade. His father was a semi-pro rugby player (athletic pedigree) and veterinarian (middle-class stability). His 6'6" frame and powerful game gave him a physical edge. By 20, he won the US Open, defeating both Nadal and Federer. The Tandil ecosystem, with its concentration of elite peers and dedicated coaching, was his primary advantage.
starting_point: Born in Tandil, Argentina in 1988 to Daniel del Potro, a semi-pro rugby player and veterinarian, and Patricia Lucas, a teacher; grew up in an unusual tennis hotbed city of 100,000 that produced six ATP tour players.
current_position: Retired professional tennis player; US Open champion (2009); career-high world No. 3 (2018); Olympic silver (2016) and bronze (2012) medalist; led Argentina to 2016 Davis Cup title; made final professional appearance at the 2022 US Open due to chronic injuries.

name: Walter Bonatti
milestone_by_age_26: Made the first ascent of the east face of the Grand Capucin in the Mont Blanc massif in 1951 at age 21, described by Hermann Buhl as 'the most difficult granite climb in an absolute sense'; also completed the fourth ascent of the north face of the Grandes Jorasses at 19 and was the youngest member of the 1954 Italian K2 expedition at 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Bergamo, Italy to an impoverished working-class family, Bonatti discovered climbing at 18 on the Grigna mountains. Within a year he was repeating the hardest existing routes in the Alps. He worked as a metalworker at Falck in Sesto San Giovanni and climbed on his days off. By 21, he had made the first ascent of the Grand Capucin, and at 24 he was selected for the Italian K2 expedition, surviving a legendary bivouac at 8,100 metres.
family_context_summary: Only child born in Bergamo, Lombardy, to a working-class family impoverished by WWII. His father was a fabric merchant. He worked as a metalworker at Falck in Sesto San Giovanni and climbed on Sundays, his only day off.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bergamo/Alps proximity, working-class self-creation, gymnastics background, climbing partners, WWII poverty
evidence_summary: Bonatti grew up in Bergamo, near the Italian Alps, and discovered climbing at 18. His working-class family was impoverished by WWII, and he worked as a metalworker while climbing on his only day off. His proximity to the Alps and the Italian alpine tradition was his primary geographic advantage. He developed exceptional physical strength through gymnastics and showed prodigious natural talent, repeating the hardest routes in the Alps within a year of starting. His self-taught, resource-poor background makes his rapid ascent to the elite level remarkable. He had no family wealth or climbing connections — his advantages were geographic proximity, physical talent, and extraordinary determination.
starting_point: Born in Bergamo, Italy in 1930 to an impoverished working-class family; father was a fabric merchant; WWII left the family destitute; worked as a metalworker and climbed on his days off.
current_position: Died on September 13, 2011 at age 81 in Rome; final status: widely considered one of the greatest mountaineers of all time; retired from climbing at 35 after solo winter ascent of the Matterhorn north face; later worked as journalist for Epoca magazine.

trajectory.event: Completed the fourth ascent of the north face of the Grandes Jorasses, one of the great north faces of the Alps, within a year of starting to climb.

Completed the first solo ascent of the south-west pillar of the Petit Dru over five days.

Completed the first solo winter ascent of the north face of the Matterhorn, then announced his retirement from professional climbing.
Died of pancreatic cancer in Rome.
